solution:
The lamp glows MORE BRIGHTLY.
The lamp (resistance R) and the capacitor are in series, so the impedance of the circuit is
\( Z = \sqrt{R^2 + X_C^2} \), where \( X_C = \frac{1}{2\pi f C} \).
On increasing the capacitance C, the capacitive reactance \( X_C \) DECREASES, because \( X_C \) is inversely proportional to C. Hence Z decreases, and for the same applied rms voltage the current \( i_{\mathrm{rms}} = \frac{e_{\mathrm{rms}}}{Z} \) increases.
The power dissipated in the lamp is \( i_{\mathrm{rms}}^2 R \) (an ideal capacitor dissipates none), so a larger current means more power in the lamp and therefore greater brightness.

The voltage across an inductor LEADS the current by \( 90^\circ \) while the voltage across a capacitor LAGS the current by \( 90^\circ \), so \( e_L \) and \( e_C \) are \( 180^\circ \) out of phase and act in OPPOSITE directions in the phasor diagram. They therefore subtract rather than add.
With L and R only, \( Z = \sqrt{R^2 + X_L^2} \).
With C added in series, \( Z = \sqrt{R^2 + \left( X_L - X_C \right)^2} \).
So long as \( X_C \) is smaller than \( 2X_L \), the net reactance \( \left| X_L - X_C \right| \) is smaller than \( X_L \) itself, and the impedance falls. It is least when \( X_C = X_L \), which is the resonance condition; then the reactances cancel completely and \( Z = R \), its minimum possible value.
[Note: this is why the impedance decreases, not a guarantee that it always must. If the added capacitor is small enough that \( X_C > 2X_L \), the net reactance again exceeds \( X_L \) and the impedance rises.]

The opposition a capacitor offers to alternating current is its capacitive reactance
\( X_C = \frac{1}{\omega C} = \frac{1}{2\pi f C} \),
which is INVERSELY proportional to the frequency of the supply.
Hence as f becomes very large, \( X_C \) becomes very small and tends to zero. A circuit element offering almost no opposition to the current behaves like a plain conducting wire, so at very high frequency the capacitor acts as a pure conductor.
(The opposite limit is the DC case: \( f = 0 \) gives \( X_C = \infty \), so a capacitor blocks DC and behaves as an open circuit.)

The current flowing through a pure inductor or an ideal capacitor, which consumes no power for its maintenance in the circuit, is called wattless current (or idle current).
In such a circuit the phase difference between the emf and the current is \( \phi = 90^\circ \), so the average power over a complete cycle is
\( P_{\mathrm{av}} = e_{\mathrm{rms}}\, i_{\mathrm{rms}} \cos\phi = e_{\mathrm{rms}}\, i_{\mathrm{rms}} \cos 90^\circ = 0 \).
The current is genuinely flowing, but no net energy is drawn from the source over a cycle — energy is stored during one quarter cycle and returned during the next. Power is dissipated in a circuit only because of its resistance.

Natural (resonant) frequency of an LC circuit:
\( f_r = \frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}} \)
This is the frequency at which the charge and current in the circuit oscillate on their own between the capacitor and the inductor.
Reactance at this frequency: at \( f = f_r \) we have \( \omega_r L = \frac{1}{\omega_r C} \), that is \( X_L = X_C \). Since \( X_L \) and \( X_C \) are \( 180^\circ \) out of phase, the NET reactance of the circuit is
\( X = X_L - X_C = 0 \).
So the reactance of an LC circuit at its natural frequency is ZERO.

Before the capacitor is added — series LR circuit with \( X_L = R \):
\( Z_1 = \sqrt{R^2 + X_L^2} = \sqrt{R^2 + R^2} = R\sqrt{2} \)
\( P_1 = \cos\phi_1 = \frac{R}{Z_1} = \frac{R}{R\sqrt{2}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \)
After the capacitor is added, with \( X_C = X_L \) — this is the resonance condition, so the two reactances cancel:
\( Z_2 = \sqrt{R^2 + \left( X_L - X_C \right)^2} = \sqrt{R^2 + 0} = R \)
\( P_2 = \cos\phi_2 = \frac{R}{Z_2} = \frac{R}{R} = 1 \)
Therefore
\( \frac{P_1}{P_2} = \frac{1/\sqrt{2}}{1} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} = 0.707 \)
That is, \( P_1 : P_2 = 1 : \sqrt{2} \).

In a purely inductive circuit the current lags behind the applied emf by \( \frac{\pi}{2} \). So if
\( e = e_0 \sin \omega t \), then \( i = i_0 \sin \left( \omega t - \frac{\pi}{2} \right) = -\, i_0 \cos \omega t \)
Instantaneous power:
\( P = e\, i = \left( e_0 \sin \omega t \right)\left( -i_0 \cos \omega t \right) = -\, e_0 i_0 \sin \omega t \cos \omega t \)
Average power over one complete cycle:
\( P_{\mathrm{av}} = \frac{\int_0^T P\, \mathrm{d}t}{T} = \frac{-\, e_0 i_0 \int_0^T \sin \omega t \cos \omega t\, \mathrm{d}t}{T} \)
Using \( 2 \sin \omega t \cos \omega t = \sin 2\omega t \),
\( P_{\mathrm{av}} = -\, \frac{e_0 i_0}{2T} \int_0^T \sin 2\omega t\, \mathrm{d}t = -\, \frac{e_0 i_0}{2T} \left[ \frac{-\cos 2\omega t}{2\omega} \right]_0^T \)
Since \( \omega T = 2\pi \), \( \cos 2\omega T = \cos 4\pi = 1 = \cos 0 \), so the bracket vanishes.
\( \therefore P_{\mathrm{av}} = 0 \)
The same result follows at once from \( P_{\mathrm{av}} = e_{\mathrm{rms}}\, i_{\mathrm{rms}} \cos\phi \) with \( \phi = 90^\circ \).
Physically, the source supplies energy to the inductor's magnetic field during one quarter cycle and receives exactly the same energy back during the next, so the average power supplied over a complete cycle is zero.

In a purely capacitive circuit the current leads the applied emf by \( \frac{\pi}{2} \). So if
\( e = e_0 \sin \omega t \), then \( i = i_0 \sin \left( \omega t + \frac{\pi}{2} \right) = i_0 \cos \omega t \)
Instantaneous power:
\( P = e\, i = \left( e_0 \sin \omega t \right)\left( i_0 \cos \omega t \right) = e_0 i_0 \sin \omega t \cos \omega t = \frac{e_0 i_0}{2} \sin 2\omega t \)
Average power over one complete cycle:
\( P_{\mathrm{av}} = \frac{1}{T} \int_0^T \frac{e_0 i_0}{2} \sin 2\omega t\, \mathrm{d}t = \frac{e_0 i_0}{2T} \left[ \frac{-\cos 2\omega t}{2\omega} \right]_0^T \)
Since \( \omega T = 2\pi \), \( \cos 2\omega T = \cos 4\pi = 1 = \cos 0 \), so the bracket is zero.
\( \therefore P_{\mathrm{av}} = 0 \)
Equivalently, \( P_{\mathrm{av}} = e_{\mathrm{rms}}\, i_{\mathrm{rms}} \cos 90^\circ = 0 \).
Hence an ideal capacitor does not dissipate power. It stores energy in its electric field while charging and returns all of it to the source while discharging; the current through it is a wattless current.

(a) Let the applied emf be \( e = e_0 \sin \omega t \) and let the resulting current differ from it in phase by \( \phi \), so that \( i = i_0 \sin \left( \omega t \pm \phi \right) \), where \( \tan\phi = \frac{X_L - X_C}{R} \).
Instantaneous power:
\( P = e\, i = e_0 i_0 \sin \omega t \, \sin \left( \omega t \pm \phi \right) \)
\( = e_0 i_0 \left[ \sin^2 \omega t \cos\phi \pm \sin \omega t \cos \omega t \sin\phi \right] \)
Average over one complete cycle, using \( \frac{1}{T}\int_0^T \sin^2 \omega t\, \mathrm{d}t = \frac{1}{2} \) and \( \int_0^T \sin \omega t \cos \omega t\, \mathrm{d}t = 0 \):
\( P_{\mathrm{av}} = e_0 i_0 \left[ \cos\phi \cdot \frac{1}{2} \pm \sin\phi \cdot 0 \right] = \frac{e_0 i_0}{2} \cos\phi \)
\( \therefore P_{\mathrm{av}} = \frac{e_0}{\sqrt{2}} \cdot \frac{i_0}{\sqrt{2}} \cos\phi = e_{\mathrm{rms}}\, i_{\mathrm{rms}} \cos\phi \)
This is the true power; \( \cos\phi = \frac{R}{Z} \) is the power factor. For the case printed in the question, where the current \( I = I_0 \sin \omega t \) is in phase with the emf, \( \phi = 0 \) (the circuit is at resonance, \( X_L = X_C \)) and the expression reduces to \( P_{\mathrm{av}} = \frac{e_0 I_0}{2} \).
(b) A transmission line carries a power \( P = V_{\mathrm{rms}} I_{\mathrm{rms}} \cos\phi \), so the current needed to deliver a given power P at a given voltage is
\( I_{\mathrm{rms}} = \frac{P}{V_{\mathrm{rms}} \cos\phi} \).
The smaller the power factor \( \cos\phi \), the LARGER the current that must be carried for the same delivered power. The power wasted as heat in the line's own resistance R is \( I_{\mathrm{rms}}^2 R \), which grows as the SQUARE of that current. Hence a low power factor means a much larger \( I^2R \) loss in transmission.

a) The current is \( i = i_0 \sin \left( \omega t + \frac{\pi}{2} \right) \) while the emf is \( e = e_0 \sin \omega t \), so the current LEADS the emf by \( \frac{\pi}{2} \) (i.e. by \( 90^\circ \)). This is the behaviour of a CAPACITOR, so the device Y is a capacitor (an ideal one, since the phase difference is exactly \( 90^\circ \)).
Its reactance is the capacitive reactance
\( X_C = \frac{1}{\omega C} = \frac{1}{2\pi f C} \), measured in ohm \( ( \Omega ) \).
b) Graph of e and i against time over one cycle: both are sine curves of the same period T, drawn on the same axes. The current curve is shifted a QUARTER of a cycle \( (T/4) \) to the LEFT of the emf curve — i reaches its peak at \( t = 0 \) while e reaches its peak at \( t = T/4 \); i is zero where e is maximum, and i is maximum where e is zero.
c) Variation of reactance with frequency: \( X_C = \frac{1}{2\pi f C} \), so \( X_C \propto \frac{1}{f} \). The graph of \( X_C \) against f is a rectangular hyperbola lying in the first quadrant: it is very large as \( f \to 0 \) (a capacitor blocks DC) and falls towards zero as f becomes large, never touching either axis.
d) Phasor diagram: draw the emf phasor \( e_0 \) making an angle \( \omega t \) with the horizontal axis; the current phasor \( i_0 \) is drawn \( 90^\circ \) ANTICLOCKWISE ahead of \( e_0 \), the two rotating together anticlockwise with angular velocity \( \omega \). Their projections on the vertical axis give the instantaneous values of e and i.

Let a resistor R, a pure inductor L and an ideal capacitor C be joined in series across an alternating source. As they are in series the same current flows through all three:
\( i = i_0 \sin \omega t \)
The voltages across the three elements are
\( e_R = i R \), \( e_L = i X_L \), \( e_C = i X_C \)
but they are not in phase with one another:
- \( e_R \) is in phase with the current;
- \( e_L \) leads the current by \( 90^\circ \);
- \( e_C \) lags the current by \( 90^\circ \).
In the phasor diagram \( e_R \) is drawn along the current direction \( \overline{OA} \); \( e_L \) and \( e_C \) are \( 180^\circ \) apart, so their resultant is the single phasor \( \left( e_L - e_C \right) \) at right angles to \( \overline{OA} \).
The applied emf is the resultant of these two perpendicular phasors, i.e. the diagonal of the rectangle:
\( e_0 = \sqrt{e_R^2 + \left( e_L - e_C \right)^2} \)
\( = \sqrt{\left( i_0 R \right)^2 + \left( i_0 X_L - i_0 X_C \right)^2} \)
\( = i_0 \sqrt{R^2 + \left( X_L - X_C \right)^2} \)
\( \therefore \frac{e_0}{i_0} = \sqrt{R^2 + \left( X_L - X_C \right)^2} \)
Comparing this with Ohm's law \( \frac{V}{i} = R \), the quantity on the right is the effective opposition of the whole circuit. It is called the IMPEDANCE Z:
\( Z = \sqrt{R^2 + \left( X_L - X_C \right)^2} = \sqrt{R^2 + \left( \omega L - \frac{1}{\omega C} \right)^2} \)
Its SI unit is the ohm \( ( \Omega ) \). The current differs in phase from the emf by \( \phi \), where \( \tan\phi = \frac{X_L - X_C}{R} \).

| Resistance | Reactance |
|---|---|
| Equally effective for AC and DC. | Affects (reduces) the current, but no energy is consumed — no heat is generated. Any energy consumed by a coil is due to its resistive component. |
| Its value is independent of the frequency of the AC. | Inductive reactance \( \left( X_L = 2\pi f L \right) \) is directly proportional to the frequency, and capacitive reactance \( \left( X_C = \frac{1}{2\pi f C} \right) \) is inversely proportional to the frequency of the AC. |
| The current opposed by a resistor is in phase with the voltage. | The current opposed by a pure inductor lags the voltage by \( \frac{\pi}{2} \), while that opposed by a pure capacitor leads the voltage by \( \frac{\pi}{2} \). |
| Denoted by R; it dissipates energy as heat \( \left( i^2 R \right) \). | Denoted by \( X_L \) or \( X_C \); it stores energy and returns it to the source. |

Both are measured in the same SI unit, the ohm \( ( \Omega ) \), and both have the same dimensions.

Let an alternating emf \( e = e_0 \sin \omega t \) be applied to a circuit containing a pure inductor L of negligible resistance.
As the current changes, a back emf \( e' = -L \frac{\mathrm{d}i}{\mathrm{d}t} \) is induced. Since the circuit has no resistance, Kirchhoff's voltage law gives \( e = -e' \), that is
\( e = L \frac{\mathrm{d}i}{\mathrm{d}t} \)
\( \therefore \mathrm{d}i = \frac{e}{L} \mathrm{d}t = \frac{e_0 \sin \omega t}{L}\, \mathrm{d}t \)
Integrating both sides,
\( i = \frac{e_0}{L} \left[ \frac{-\cos \omega t}{\omega} \right] + \text{constant} \)
As the emf oscillates about zero, the current must also oscillate about zero, so there can be no time-independent component; the constant of integration is zero.
\( \therefore i = \frac{-e_0}{\omega L} \cos \omega t = \frac{e_0}{\omega L} \sin \left( \omega t - \frac{\pi}{2} \right) \)
\( \therefore i = i_0 \sin \left( \omega t - \frac{\pi}{2} \right) \), where \( i_0 = \frac{e_0}{\omega L} \)
Comparing \( e = e_0 \sin \omega t \) with \( i = i_0 \sin \left( \omega t - \frac{\pi}{2} \right) \): the current reaches any given phase a quarter of a cycle AFTER the voltage does. Hence in a purely inductive AC circuit the current lags behind the voltage by \( \frac{\pi}{2} \), or equivalently the voltage is ahead of the current by \( \frac{\pi}{2} \) in phase.

Let \( e = e_0 \sin \omega t \) be applied across a capacitor of capacitance C. At any instant the potential difference across the plates equals the applied emf, so the charge on the capacitor is
\( q = Ce = C e_0 \sin \omega t \)
The current is the rate of flow of charge:
\( i = \frac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t} = \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t} \left( C e_0 \sin \omega t \right) = \omega C e_0 \cos \omega t \)
\( = \frac{e_0}{\left( 1/\omega C \right)} \cos \omega t \)
Using \( \cos \omega t = \sin \left( \omega t + \frac{\pi}{2} \right) \),
\( \therefore i = \frac{e_0}{X_C} \sin \left( \omega t + \frac{\pi}{2} \right) = i_0 \sin \left( \omega t + \frac{\pi}{2} \right) \)
where \( i_0 = \frac{e_0}{X_C} \) and \( X_C = \frac{1}{\omega C} \) is the capacitive reactance.
Graph of e and i against \( \omega t \): both are sine curves of the same period drawn on one pair of axes, with the current curve shifted \( \frac{\pi}{2} \) to the LEFT of the emf curve. Starting at \( \omega t = 0 \): i is at its positive peak \( i_0 \) while e is zero; at \( \omega t = \frac{\pi}{2} \), e is at its peak \( e_0 \) while i is zero; at \( \omega t = \pi \), i is at its negative peak while e is zero again. The current therefore leads the emf by a quarter of a cycle throughout.
